newsitem.title: GERMANY: Deutsche Telekom counts hours to opening bell.
newsitem.headline: Deutsche Telekom counts hours to opening bell.

text.p: German phone giant Deutsche Telekom AG and its new investors were counting down the hours to the opening bell on the Frankfurt stock exchange on Monday as Europe's largest ever share offering was set to begin trade.

In contrast to the 19th century Italian renaissance-style stock exchange, Telekom lined the front of the bourse with glowing magenta cubes, meant to symbolise data bits heralding the information age of the 21st century.

The words "Here we are..." radiated into the night from a wide-TV screen in front of the bourse, with a Times Square- style clock ticking off the hours and minutes until the stock market's opening, launching a new era in German industry.
"If this is a succesful privatisation it could really get the German market going, creating a broad equity culture," said Jonathan Shantry, European telecoms analyst with Credit Lyonnais in London.

At the weekend, Telekom and the banks leading its share offer set the issue price at 28.50 marks, making the issue worth some 20 billion marks ($13.3 billion), second only to the huge listing of Japan's Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corp.

The issue price is lower than expected, leaving plenty of room for the share price to rise quickly when official trading begins, equity analysts said. In unofficial "grey market" trade ahead of the issue, Telekom shares have been trading at around 34 marks. Analysts expect the share to open at around 33 marks.

Shares will trade on all eight of Germany's regional stock exchanges with the first price quotes expected by mid-morning and will move to the New York Stock Exchange later in the day when Telekom shares are listed there for the first time.
On Tuesday, Telekom shares will trade on the Tokyo Stock Exchange in what could be Japan's largest ever foreign listing.
With annual sales of 66 billion marks, Deutsche Telekom is Europe's largest telecommunications group and one of Germany's biggest corporations.
Bankers have heralded its listing as a watershed event for Germany's financial markets as the enormous public interest in the issue has attracted some two million private investors.

Private investors, stereotyped as cautious and afraid of high-stakes gambling on the stock market, caught investment fever with Telekom's issue, cracking open piggy banks in a bid to cash in on what has been sold as a sure thing.

With a third of the issue placed abroad, the Telekom offering also marks a huge infusion of foreign capital into Germany, a fact that could indicate heightened interest by foreign investors in German share issues.
While some analysts considered the issue price to be fair, others thought it was still too expensive compared to other international phone companies and urged caution.

The moment of truth will come quickly enough and investors are bracing for a roller-coaster ride this week as Telekom's share joins the German DAX index of 30 blue chips, settling in as one of Europe's most highly-valued public companies.
